analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $7.25 an hour and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar in May 2005 but never reached a committee vote or the Senate floor, and the federal minimum wage stayed at $5.15 for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 an hour in three steps: to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 over about two years [S2][S3]. It would also, for the first time, apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, phasing the local wage up from $3.55 by 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal level [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced with 37 cosponsors, all Democrats or the chamber's one Independent, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the Congress ended in January 2007 with the minimum wage unchanged [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning between $5.15 and $7.25 an hour would get raises in three steps, including workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, where the local minimum wage was far below the federal level.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25, in steps over about two years, lifting pay for workers at the bottom of the wage scale.
Extends federal minimum wage law to the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, where the minimum was $3.55, phasing it up by 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay near the minimum wage — restaurants, retail, and small businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost may be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: Higher wage floors raise payroll costs for businesses that employ many minimum-wage workers, and the increase would be largest for small employers in low-cost areas; some economists argue a higher wage floor reduces entry-level jobs, though the bill's phase-in over two years softens the immediate impact.

The Northern Mariana Islands provision would raise wages in an isolated island economy by roughly doubling them over a transition period, a cost borne locally by employers there, though the bill explicitly stages the increase in small 50-cent steps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is a higher guaranteed wage for low-paid workers against higher labor costs for low-wage employers. The two-year phase-in and the small, staggered steps for the islands reduce disruption. The bill was straightforward and narrowly drawn: no tax offsets, no exemptions, just a wage floor increase.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never took it up — no committee vote, no floor vote — and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2005 on May 18, 2005, with 30 original Senate cosponsors listed in the bill text.
The Senate read the bill a second time and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on May 19, 2005, Calendar No. 109 — a step that does not by itself bring a bill to the floor.
The bill gathered 37 cosponsors, 36 Democrats and one Independent; no Republican cosponsored it.
After being placed on the calendar, the bill received no further action — no committee markup, no procedural vote, no floor vote — and died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum wage kept paying $5.15 an hour, the rate in effect since 1997, for the rest of the Congress. Workers at the bottom of the wage scale gained nothing; a higher minimum wage was enacted the following Congress, after this bill had expired.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that pay the minimum wage

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 30 original cosponsors.

for.name: 36 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership (Majority Leader Bill Frist)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years after it was placed on the calendar; the majority leader controls what gets floor time.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's sole Independent; no vote ever occurred, so opposition is shown by the bill's failure to reach the floor rather than by recorded votes.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, fast food, small business)
industries.note: The bill would raise the wage floor these employers must pay from $5.15 toward $7.25 over two years. The gain to low-wage workers comes directly out of payroll budgets that these industries have an interest in keeping low.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and tourism employers
industries.note: The CNMI had long been exempt from the federal minimum wage, paying $3.55 an hour. The bill would phase that up to the federal wage, a significant cost to island employers, particularly its garment industry.
